# Chapter 5 — Group Policy Objects — The Configuration Inheritance Engine

::: {.callout-note}
## In this chapter
How Group Policy delivers Windows configuration through structural OU
inheritance, the breadth of the configuration surface it covers, and why the
model is both powerful and — in the contemporary, partly-disconnected
environment — opaque and difficult to audit.
:::

## Architecture and Native Capabilities

Group Policy Objects (GPOs) are the primary mechanism by which Windows system configuration is applied to domain-joined machines and users in an Active Directory environment. A GPO is a **paired data structure**:

* **Group Policy Container (GPC)** — stored in the Active Directory domain partition, holding metadata such as the GPO's GUID, version number, and security descriptor.
* **Group Policy Template (GPT)** — stored in the `SYSVOL` share of every domain controller, holding the actual policy settings files, ADMX-based administrative template definitions, scripts, and software installation packages.

GPOs are created and managed through the Group Policy Management Console (GPMC), which presents the combined view of both storage locations. A GPO has no effect until it is **linked** to a site, domain, or Organizational Unit. Linking a GPO to an OU is the act that causes the policy to apply to objects within that OU and, by inheritance, to objects within all child OUs — subject to filtering and precedence rules.

The inheritance model is the defining characteristic of the system. When the Group Policy Client service applies policy, it walks up the OU hierarchy from the object's container to the domain root, collecting all linked GPOs at each level and building an ordered list that reflects the inheritance hierarchy.

```text
Evaluation order (later wins on conflict):
   Site-linked GPOs
        ▼
   Domain-linked GPOs
        ▼
   OU-linked GPOs (parent OU)
        ▼
   OU-linked GPOs (child OU)   ← highest precedence
```

Two filtering mechanisms refine this default flow:

* **WMI filters** condition a GPO's application on the result of a WMI query against the target machine, scoping a GPO to machines meeting specific hardware or software conditions without managing separate OUs for each condition.
* **Security filtering** controls which principals actually receive a GPO by requiring both *Read* and *Apply Group Policy* permissions on the GPO object; removing *Apply Group Policy* from a group exempts its members from the policy regardless of their OU position.

## Policy Scope and Coverage

The breadth of GPO coverage across the Windows configuration surface is comprehensive, split into two halves:

* **Computer configuration** applies to the machine at startup regardless of which user logs on. It covers security settings (account policy, local policies, audit policy, user-rights assignments, security options), software installation, startup/shutdown scripts, computer-side folder redirection, Windows Firewall rules, certificate distribution through auto-enrollment and trusted-root configuration, and the full body of Administrative Template settings exposing registry-backed OS configuration.
* **User configuration** applies when a specific user logs on, covering analogous software, script, folder-redirection, and Administrative Template settings scoped to user-side registry paths and Windows features.

The **Administrative Templates** model lets any vendor or organization extend the policy schema by depositing ADMX and ADML files in the SYSVOL Central Store, making new settings available to all administrators through the GPMC without modifying the schema or the AD directory itself.

## Limitations of Group Policy in the Contemporary Environment

Group Policy is **exclusively an on-premises, domain-joined construct.** Its application mechanism requires that the machine be able to communicate with a domain controller at startup and at logon:

* Non-domain-joined devices receive no Group Policy.
* Cloud-native workloads that are not domain-connected receive no Group Policy.
* Managed mobile devices — iOS, Android — receive no Group Policy.
* A domain-joined machine separated from domain controllers by an unreliable WAN link processes cached policy at startup but cannot retrieve updates until connectivity is restored; policy on a machine off-network for an extended period may be materially stale, and no native mechanism continuously verifies the currency of applied policy against the currently-linked GPOs.

> **The auditability gap:** A machine's effective configuration is the combined effect of all applicable GPOs, the WMI and security-filter conditions that may or may not have evaluated as expected, the precedence resolution among conflicting settings, and the client-side-extension processing of each policy area. No single system presents this without querying the target machine.

The consequences for assurance are concrete. The `gpresult` command reports the GPOs that applied and the resulting settings, but it must be run on or against the target machine and reflects the state at the last refresh cycle. GPOs are not version-controlled by any native mechanism — the GPMC can back up and restore GPOs, but a backup is a point-in-time snapshot, not a versioned history. There is no native diff between two versions of a GPO's settings, no change log beyond the modification timestamp on the GPO Container object, and no preview of the combined effect of all applicable GPOs before they reach a machine. Group Policy is, in this precise sense, an opaque, distributed, and difficult-to-audit configuration system whose actual enforcement state is known only to the endpoints that have applied it.
